I am watching closely for any sign of tubal rupture such as worsening pain, dizziness, or hypotension, because that would mean she needs immediate resuscitation with IV fluids, a type and crossmatch, and emergent surgery. I would also check her Rh status and give Rh immunoglobulin if she is Rh negative, since that matters for future pregnancies regardless of this pregnancy's outcome. Until gynecology has definitively assessed her I am not comfortable discharging her home.

title: Pregnant Woman with Severe Headache at 34 Weeks
reading_stem: A 27 year old woman at 34 weeks gestation presents with a severe headache, visual spots, and epigastric discomfort for several hours. She has had no prenatal complications noted so far. Vitals are BP 168/108, HR 90, RR 18, with 2+ pitting edema in her legs.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate asks for a repeat blood pressure, confirm sustained severe hypertension above 160/110 on a second reading. If the candidate orders urinalysis and bloodwork, reveal significant proteinuria, elevated liver enzymes, and a platelet count of 95, consistent with severe pre-eclampsia with features suggestive of evolving HELLP syndrome. If the candidate starts IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and an antihypertensive such as labetalol or hydralazine to control severe range blood pressure, allow blood pressure to improve into a safer range. If the candidate delays magnesium and antihypertensive treatment to pursue extensive additional workup first, have the patient develop a generalized tonic clonic seizure at minute 9 to simulate eclampsia, requiring the candidate to manage the airway, give magnesium, and stabilize before urgent delivery planning. If the candidate calls obstetrics urgently and discusses the need for delivery given severe features, this is correct regardless of gestational age at this severity. Reward candidates who recognize severe range blood pressure with symptoms as an emergency requiring magnesium sulfate regardless of whether an actual seizure has occurred, who treat blood pressure promptly, and who involve obstetrics immediately for consideration of delivery.
checklist: Recognizes severe pre-eclampsia from severe range blood pressure with headache, visual changes, and epigastric pain
Starts magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis without waiting for an actual seizure
Treats severe range hypertension promptly with an appropriate antihypertensive such as labetalol or hydralazine
Manages eclamptic seizure with airway protection and magnesium if it occurs
Involves obstetrics urgently given severe features and the likely need for delivery
model_answer: Severe range blood pressure with headache, visual changes, and epigastric pain at 34 weeks tells me this is severe pre-eclampsia until proven otherwise, and I need to treat this as an emergency rather than wait for a seizure to happen. I would start magnesium sulfate immediately for seizure prophylaxis, since that is indicated based on severity of features alone, and give an antihypertensive like labetalol or hydralazine to bring her blood pressure out of the severe range safely. I am sending bloodwork and urine looking for proteinuria, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets because this pattern raises concern for HELLP syndrome, which changes urgency. If she seizes despite my efforts I would protect her airway, ensure she is receiving magnesium, and treat this as eclampsia. I am calling obstetrics urgently because severe pre-eclampsia at this gestational age with these features usually means delivery needs to be seriously considered very soon.

title: Febrile Infant Under 90 Days Old
reading_stem: A 6 week old boy is brought in by his parents for fever measured at home to 38.4C rectally. He has been feeding slightly less than usual but has no cough, rash, or vomiting. He appears well in his mother's arms. Vitals in the department confirm temperature 38.3C, HR 160, RR 40.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate performs a full septic workup discussion, describe a well appearing infant on exam with no focal source found. If the candidate orders blood cultures, urine obtained by catheterization, inflammatory markers, and considers a validated risk-stratification approach such as Step by Step, PECARN, or Rochester criteria appropriate for this 29 to 90 day age band, confirm this is the correct approach, since he is not a neonate under 28 days who would require an automatic full workup and admission regardless of any test result. Allow discussion of the workup results and reveal a positive urinalysis suggestive of a urinary tract infection with clean catch not otherwise contaminated. If the candidate proposes discharge home without antibiotics or without any workup due to the infant looking well, interject that even well-appearing infants in this age band require a structured risk-stratification workup before any disposition decision, and have blood culture eventually grow a pathogen overnight to underscore the risk of skipping the workup entirely. Correct management includes recognizing this age group is risk-stratified using validated criteria rather than either a blanket neonatal-style admission or reassurance from appearance alone, and that this particular infant needs empiric antibiotics and admission because his workup found a urinary tract infection, not simply because of his age.
checklist: Recognizes that infants 29 to 90 days old are risk-stratified using validated criteria (such as Rochester or Step by Step) rather than managed with the same blanket regardless-of-appearance rule as neonates under 28 days
Obtains blood culture, catheterized urine studies, and considers lumbar puncture for CSF
Applies validated risk stratification criteria appropriately rather than relying on gestalt alone
Starts empiric antibiotics after cultures are obtained rather than deferring treatment
Admits the infant for observation rather than discharging home
model_answer: Even though this baby looks well, at 6 weeks old he falls in the 29 to 90 day age band where I cannot rely on appearance alone to exclude serious bacterial infection, so I am pursuing a structured workup including blood cultures, a catheterized urine sample, inflammatory markers, and consideration of a lumbar puncture for CSF studies. I would use a validated approach such as Step by Step or PECARN criteria to help risk stratify him, since he is not a neonate under 28 days who would need an automatic full workup and admission regardless of any test result. Once his urinalysis suggests a urinary tract infection, that finding on its own supports starting empiric antibiotics after cultures are obtained and admitting him for observation, rather than the age cutoff alone driving that decision. If his full workup had come back reassuring and he met low risk criteria, a more selective approach could reasonably be considered for an infant his age. I am planning to admit him now because his urinalysis result places him outside low risk, and I would keep him admitted pending full culture results and clinical course.

title: Woman with Injuries Inconsistent with Stated Mechanism
reading_stem: A 33 year old woman presents with facial bruising and a wrist injury, stating she fell down the stairs. Her partner is present and answers most questions for her. On exam she has bruising in different stages of healing and appears anxious and avoids eye contact.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate asks to speak with the patient alone, describe the partner initially resisting but eventually agreeing to step out after the candidate explains this is routine practice for all patients. Once alone, if the candidate asks open, nonjudgmental questions about safety at home, reveal that she discloses ongoing physical abuse from her partner and expresses fear of retaliation if he finds out she said anything. If the candidate validates her disclosure without judgment and assesses immediate safety including whether children are in the home and whether the partner has access to weapons, allow her to share that there are two children at home and the partner owns a firearm, both of which raise the risk level significantly. If the candidate fails to separate her from the partner and asks about the injury mechanism in his presence, she minimizes and denies any concern, and the encounter ends without disclosure or a safety plan, representing a missed opportunity that should be identified afterward. If disclosure occurs, expect the candidate to discuss documentation of injuries, referral to social work or a domestic violence advocate, and collaborative safety planning that respects her autonomy rather than mandating an immediate action she is not ready for, while discussing local reporting obligations regarding children in the home.
checklist: Recognizes injury patterns and partner behavior as red flags for intimate partner violence
Separates the patient from her partner to allow private, confidential disclosure
Uses open, nonjudgmental questioning to screen for abuse and assesses immediate safety including children and weapons
Involves social work or a domestic violence advocate and documents findings thoroughly
Develops a collaborative safety plan that respects patient autonomy while addressing any child safety reporting obligations
model_answer: The pattern of injuries at different stages of healing along with her partner speaking for her and her guarded body language raises my concern for intimate partner violence, so my first step is finding a reason to speak with her privately, separate from her partner. Once we are alone I would ask open, nonjudgmental questions about her safety at home rather than leading questions, and if she discloses abuse I would validate that disclosure and let her know I believe her and that help is available. I need to assess immediate risk, including whether children are in the home and whether her partner has access to weapons, since both significantly change the urgency of safety planning. I would document her injuries carefully and objectively and involve social work or a domestic violence advocate to help build a safety plan that she is comfortable with, rather than forcing an action she is not ready to take. Given that children are in the home, I would also consider my reporting obligations regarding child safety while continuing to support her autonomy in her own decisions.

title: Toddler with Severe Dehydration from Gastroenteritis
reading_stem: A 14 month old girl presents with 3 days of vomiting and watery diarrhea. Her mother reports she has had minimal urine output today and seems very sleepy. On exam she has sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, and delayed capillary refill. Vitals are HR 170, BP 78/44, RR 34.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate assesses for shock, confirm delayed capillary refill of 4 seconds, mottled skin, and lethargy consistent with decompensated hypovolemic shock. If the candidate gives a rapid isotonic fluid bolus, describe modest improvement in heart rate and mental status, and expect the candidate to reassess after each bolus rather than giving one bolus and moving on. If repeat boluses are needed, allow up to 2 to 3 boluses with reassessment between each, watching for signs of fluid overload such as new crackles or hepatomegaly. If the candidate checks a point of care glucose, reveal a low value consistent with hypoglycemia from poor intake, requiring dextrose correction. If the candidate does not reassess after the first bolus and instead moves on to other tasks, have the child's mental status remain poor and heart rate stay elevated to prompt reassessment. If the candidate considers electrolyte and venous blood gas testing, reveal a metabolic acidosis and mild hyponatremia consistent with the degree of dehydration. Correct management includes recognizing decompensated shock, rapid isotonic fluid boluses with frequent reassessment, correction of hypoglycemia, and admission for ongoing rehydration and monitoring, with consideration of a pediatric intensive care unit if she does not stabilize after initial boluses.
checklist: Recognizes decompensated hypovolemic shock from history and exam findings
Gives rapid isotonic fluid boluses with reassessment after each one rather than a single bolus alone
Checks and corrects point of care glucose given risk of hypoglycemia in a poorly feeding, vomiting child
Monitors for signs of fluid overload while resuscitating aggressively
Arranges appropriate admission, including pediatric intensive care if she remains unstable after initial resuscitation
model_answer: This child has decompensated hypovolemic shock from severe gastroenteritis, shown by her tachycardia, low blood pressure, delayed capillary refill, and lethargy, so my priority is rapid isotonic fluid resuscitation rather than maintenance fluids. I would give a fluid bolus and reassess her heart rate, capillary refill, and mental status right after, repeating boluses as needed while watching for signs of fluid overload like new crackles or an enlarging liver. Given her poor intake and vomiting I want a point of care glucose checked right away, and if she is hypoglycemic I would correct that promptly since it can worsen her mental status independently. I would also send a venous blood gas and electrolytes to understand her acid base and sodium status, which helps guide ongoing fluid management. Given how sick she is, I am planning to admit her, and if she does not respond adequately to initial boluses I would escalate to pediatric intensive care rather than continuing to manage her on a general ward.

title: Young Adult with Fever, Rash, and Neck Stiffness
reading_stem: A 19 year old university student presents with fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness for 6 hours. His roommate noticed a spreading purpuric rash on his legs this morning. He looks unwell and is reluctant to move his neck. Vitals are HR 132, BP 90/58, RR 26, temp 39.4C.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate examines the skin, confirm a rapidly spreading nonblanching purpuric rash on the lower extremities and trunk. If the candidate recognizes this as likely meningococcemia and starts empiric antibiotics such as ceftriaxone immediately without waiting for lumbar puncture or imaging, allow the patient to begin stabilizing over the following minutes with fluid resuscitation. If the candidate delays antibiotics to first obtain a CT head and lumbar puncture, have the patient's blood pressure drop further and rash spread more extensively to simulate the danger of delaying antibiotics in suspected meningococcemia, since empiric treatment should never wait for confirmatory testing in this presentation. If the candidate considers droplet or airborne precautions and notifies public health given the diagnosis, this is correct and should be reinforced as necessary given the contagious nature and public health reporting obligations for meningococcal disease. If the candidate asks about contacts, reveal his roommate and girlfriend as close contacts who would need prophylactic antibiotics. If the candidate performs blood cultures before antibiotics without delaying treatment meaningfully, that is appropriate. Expect discussion of aggressive fluid resuscitation for septic shock, ICU level care, and coordination with public health for contact prophylaxis and case reporting.
checklist: Recognizes the combination of fever, meningismus, and purpuric rash as likely meningococcemia
Starts empiric antibiotics immediately without delaying for lumbar puncture or imaging
Resuscitates aggressively for septic shock while obtaining blood cultures without meaningfully delaying antibiotics
Implements appropriate droplet precautions and recognizes the public health reporting obligation
Identifies close contacts requiring prophylactic antibiotics
model_answer: Fever, neck stiffness, and a rapidly spreading purpuric rash in a young adult is meningococcemia until proven otherwise, and this is a situation where I am giving empiric antibiotics like ceftriaxone immediately rather than waiting for a lumbar puncture or CT head, because any delay in antibiotics increases mortality significantly. I would draw blood cultures quickly if it does not meaningfully delay treatment, but I am not holding antibiotics for that. Given his hypotension and tachycardia I would resuscitate him aggressively as I would any septic shock patient, with fluids and likely escalation to vasopressors and ICU care if he does not respond. I would put droplet precautions in place immediately given the risk of transmission, and I know this is a reportable disease so I would notify public health promptly. I would also identify close contacts like his roommate and girlfriend so they can receive prophylactic antibiotics as soon as possible.

title: Woman with Pleuritic Chest Pain After Long Flight
reading_stem: A 46 year old woman presents with sudden pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath that began a few hours after a 12 hour international flight. She has mild right calf swelling and tenderness. Vitals are HR 118, BP 122/78, RR 24, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate calculates a pretest probability score such as the Wells criteria, reveal findings supporting a moderate to high pretest probability given recent immobilization, tachycardia, and unilateral leg swelling. If the candidate orders a CT pulmonary angiogram, reveal findings of a segmental pulmonary embolism without evidence of right heart strain on the study, and normal troponin, consistent with a low-risk PE given the absence of any RV dysfunction or biomarker elevation despite normal vitals. If the candidate starts anticoagulation promptly with a direct oral anticoagulant or heparin, allow stabilization. If the candidate considers thrombolysis at this stage, redirect by revealing the patient remains hemodynamically stable with no right ventricular strain, meaning thrombolysis is not indicated and anticoagulation alone is appropriate, testing whether the candidate over-treats a low-risk, hemodynamically stable PE. If the candidate does not consider PE at all and instead treats for musculoskeletal pain, have the patient develop worsening hypoxia and tachycardia at minute 9 to force recognition. Expect discussion of risk stratification tools such as the PESI score to help decide on outpatient versus inpatient management, and consideration of provoked versus unprovoked PE given the recent flight as a transient risk factor influencing duration of anticoagulation.
checklist: Uses a validated pretest probability tool such as Wells criteria to guide the diagnostic pathway
Confirms the diagnosis with CT pulmonary angiogram and assesses for right heart strain and troponin elevation
Correctly classifies a PE with no RV strain and a normal troponin as low-risk, distinguishing it from submassive (intermediate-risk) PE which requires RV dysfunction or biomarker elevation
Starts appropriate anticoagulation without unnecessary escalation to thrombolysis in a stable patient
Uses a risk stratification tool such as PESI to help decide on disposition and considers duration of anticoagulation given the provoked nature of this event
model_answer: Given her recent long flight, unilateral leg swelling, tachycardia, and pleuritic chest pain, I have a moderate to high pretest probability for pulmonary embolism using something like the Wells criteria, so I am proceeding to a CT pulmonary angiogram to confirm the diagnosis. If that confirms a segmental PE without right heart strain and her troponin is normal, I am classifying her as low-risk PE, since she has neither RV dysfunction on imaging nor a positive biomarker, and I am not going to reach for thrombolysis, since that carries bleeding risk that is not justified here. My management is anticoagulation, either with a direct oral anticoagulant or heparin depending on other factors, started promptly once the diagnosis is confirmed. I would use a tool like the PESI score to help decide whether she can be managed as an outpatient or needs admission, and given her overall stability and low-risk classification she may be a candidate for outpatient management with close follow up. I would also note this appears to be a provoked event related to prolonged immobility, which matters for how long she ultimately needs to stay on anticoagulation.

title: Facial Trauma with Impending Airway Compromise
reading_stem: A 34 year old man arrives after a motorcycle collision with significant facial trauma including a fractured mandible and bleeding into the oropharynx. He is agitated, has gurgling respirations, and is difficult to understand. Vitals are HR 122, BP 128/82, RR 28, oxygen saturation 90 percent on high flow oxygen.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate performs suction of the airway, describe ongoing brisk oral bleeding that quickly re-accumulates, making visualization difficult. If the candidate identifies this as a difficult airway due to facial trauma, bleeding, and distorted anatomy, and calls for backup including anesthesia or the most experienced airway provider available along with preparation of a surgical airway kit, allow this preparation to proceed appropriately. If the candidate attempts a standard rapid sequence intubation without a clear backup plan or surgical airway readiness, describe a failed first attempt due to blood obscuring the view, forcing the candidate to move to a rescue strategy, testing whether they had a plan in place before starting. If the candidate uses video laryngoscopy with continuous suction available and has a bougie ready, allow successful intubation on either the first or second attempt. If oxygen saturation continues to fall during attempts, expect the candidate to call for a surgical airway such as cricothyrotomy given a cannot intubate cannot oxygenate scenario. Expect discussion of preoxygenation, positioning, and having a structured backup plan clearly verbalized before the first attempt, consistent with a difficult airway algorithm approach.
checklist: Recognizes this as a predicted difficult airway due to facial trauma, bleeding, and distorted anatomy
Calls for additional skilled airway help and prepares a surgical airway kit before attempting intubation
Verbalizes a structured backup plan before the first intubation attempt rather than improvising after failure
Uses appropriate airway adjuncts such as video laryngoscopy, continuous suction, and a bougie
Escalates to a surgical airway if a cannot intubate cannot oxygenate situation develops
model_answer: This is a predicted difficult airway given his facial trauma, active oral bleeding, and distorted anatomy, so before I do anything I want to call for the most experienced airway provider available and have a surgical airway kit opened and ready at the bedside. I would preoxygenate as best I can, position him appropriately, and use continuous suction along with video laryngoscopy and a bougie ready to go, since blood is likely to obscure my view. I am verbalizing my backup plan out loud before I ever attempt intubation, because if my first attempt fails I do not want to be improvising in the moment. If I cannot intubate and cannot adequately oxygenate him, I am moving to a surgical airway without hesitation rather than making repeated attempts at oral intubation. Throughout this I am also thinking about who else needs to be in the room, including anesthesia or ENT, given how high risk this airway is.

title: Rapidly Progressive Angioedema on an ACE Inhibitor
reading_stem: A 58 year old man on lisinopril presents with progressive lip and tongue swelling that started 2 hours ago. His voice now sounds muffled and he is drooling. He denies hives or itching. Vitals are HR 104, BP 138/86, RR 22, oxygen saturation 96 percent.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate examines the oropharynx, describe significant tongue and soft palate edema with a muffled voice and increasing work of breathing, but no urticaria, supporting ACE inhibitor induced angioedema rather than allergic anaphylaxis. If the candidate gives epinephrine, antihistamines, and steroids reflexively as if this were anaphylaxis, allow these to be given but reveal minimal to no improvement in the swelling over the following minutes, since bradykinin mediated angioedema does not reliably respond to these treatments, and the true priority is airway management. If the candidate recognizes progressive airway compromise and prepares for early, awake intubation given predicted rapid worsening, or calls for anesthesia or ENT for awake fiberoptic intubation while the airway is still manageable, reward this as the correct approach. If the candidate waits to intubate until the airway is nearly obstructed, describe a much more difficult, high risk airway attempt with significant desaturation, illustrating why early intervention before complete obstruction is critical in progressive angioedema. If icatibant or fresh frozen plasma is mentioned as a bradykinin pathway specific treatment where available, acknowledge this as an appropriate adjunct while emphasizing airway security remains the priority. Correct disposition is ICU admission for close airway monitoring regardless of whether intubation occurs.
checklist: Distinguishes ACE inhibitor induced angioedema from allergic anaphylaxis based on absence of urticaria and lack of response to epinephrine
Recognizes progressive airway swelling as an indication for early, controlled airway management rather than waiting
Calls for awake or fiberoptic intubation with experienced airway support while the airway is still manageable
Considers bradykinin pathway specific treatments such as icatibant or FFP where available as adjuncts, not substitutes for airway security
Arranges ICU admission for close airway monitoring regardless of whether intubation was performed
model_answer: The absence of hives or itching along with his ACE inhibitor use makes me think this is bradykinin mediated angioedema rather than classic allergic anaphylaxis, which matters because epinephrine, antihistamines, and steroids are unlikely to reliably reverse this swelling. Given that his tongue and soft palate swelling are progressing and his voice is already muffled, I am not going to wait until he is in extremis to secure his airway, I want to call for an experienced airway provider now for an early, controlled, likely awake or fiberoptic intubation while he can still cooperate and while anatomy is still manageable. If a bradykinin specific treatment like icatibant or fresh frozen plasma is available I would consider it as an adjunct, but I am not relying on it to avoid needing to protect his airway. I would still give epinephrine, antihistamines, and steroids as reasonable adjuncts in case there is any allergic component, but my main focus is airway security. Whether or not he ends up intubated, I am admitting him to an ICU setting for close airway monitoring given how quickly this can progress.

title: Procedural Sedation for Shoulder Dislocation Reduction
reading_stem: A 26 year old healthy man presents with an anterior shoulder dislocation after a fall while playing basketball. He is in significant pain and the joint needs reduction. He last ate a full meal about one hour ago. Vitals are HR 98, BP 128/80, RR 18, oxygen saturation 99 percent.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate performs a pre-sedation assessment including airway examination, fasting status, and ASA classification, note he is ASA I but has a recent full meal, and expect discussion of how this affects risk versus benefit rather than being an absolute contraindication to emergency procedural sedation. If the candidate discusses monitoring requirements including continuous pulse oximetry, capnography if available, blood pressure, and dedicated personnel for airway management, confirm these are set up appropriately. If the candidate chooses a sedation agent such as ketamine, propofol, or a ketamine-propofol combination and dosing is discussed reasonably, allow the procedure to proceed with adequate sedation achieved. If the candidate fails to prepare airway equipment and reversal or rescue plans before sedating, interject that during the procedure the patient develops transient oxygen desaturation, testing whether the candidate has suction, bag valve mask, and airway equipment ready and responds appropriately with airway repositioning and support. If the candidate successfully reduces the shoulder and monitors recovery until the patient returns to baseline mental status before discharge, this is correct. Expect discussion of informed consent, aspiration risk given recent food intake, and appropriate recovery monitoring before discharge with post-reduction neurovascular exam and sling application.
checklist: Performs a proper pre-sedation assessment including airway exam, fasting status, and risk classification
Sets up appropriate monitoring including continuous pulse oximetry, capnography if available, and dedicated personnel
Selects and doses a sedation agent appropriately, weighing aspiration risk given recent oral intake
Has airway rescue equipment ready and responds promptly to any desaturation during the procedure
Monitors recovery to baseline before discharge and documents a post-reduction neurovascular exam
model_answer: Before I sedate him I want a full pre-sedation assessment, including his airway exam, that he ate about an hour ago, and confirming he is otherwise healthy, which I would weigh as increased aspiration risk that changes my approach rather than an absolute contraindication in this urgent situation. I would set up continuous pulse oximetry, capnography if it is available, blood pressure monitoring, and make sure I have a dedicated person focused only on airway and sedation monitoring separate from the person doing the reduction. For the agent I would consider ketamine given its relative preservation of airway reflexes, or a ketamine-propofol combination, dosed carefully and titrated to effect. Before I give anything I want suction, bag valve mask, and airway equipment at the bedside in case he desaturates or needs airway support during the procedure. After the reduction I would monitor him until he is back to his baseline mental status, do a careful neurovascular exam of the limb, and apply a sling before considering him safe for discharge.

title: Older Woman with Painful Red Eye and Blurred Vision
reading_stem: A 68 year old woman presents with a painful red right eye and blurred vision that started suddenly this evening after being in a dimly lit movie theater. She reports seeing halos around lights and has nausea and a headache. Her right eye looks injected with a hazy cornea.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate checks visual acuity, describe significantly reduced acuity in the affected eye. If the candidate palpates the globe or measures intraocular pressure, reveal a firm globe on palpation or a measured pressure markedly elevated, consistent with acute angle closure glaucoma. If the candidate examines the pupil, describe a mid dilated, poorly reactive pupil in the affected eye. If the candidate starts topical treatment such as a topical beta blocker, alpha agonist, and considers acetazolamide to lower intraocular pressure, along with urgent ophthalmology consultation, allow improvement in symptoms and pressure over time. If the candidate misdiagnoses this as simple conjunctivitis and prescribes topical antibiotics for discharge home, have the patient return in the scenario narrative with worsening vision loss and pain to illustrate the danger of a missed diagnosis and permanent vision loss risk. If the candidate discusses avoiding pupil dilating drops given the diagnosis, this is correct since dilation would worsen angle closure. Correct management is recognizing this as an ophthalmologic emergency, starting pressure lowering treatment while awaiting ophthalmology, and arranging emergent ophthalmology evaluation for definitive treatment such as laser iridotomy.
checklist: Recognizes acute angle closure glaucoma from the combination of painful red eye, halos, nausea, and a hazy cornea
Checks visual acuity and intraocular pressure or assesses globe firmness
Avoids pupil dilating drops given the diagnosis
Starts appropriate pressure lowering treatment such as topical agents and acetazolamide while awaiting ophthalmology
Arranges emergent ophthalmology consultation recognizing this as a vision threatening emergency
model_answer: A painful red eye with a hazy cornea, halos around lights, nausea, and a mid dilated poorly reactive pupil in an older patient strongly suggests acute angle closure glaucoma, which I consider a true ophthalmologic emergency because delayed treatment risks permanent vision loss. I would check her visual acuity and try to assess intraocular pressure or at least globe firmness on palpation to support the diagnosis. I am deliberately avoiding any pupil dilating drops since that would worsen the angle closure. My initial treatment would include topical agents such as a beta blocker and alpha agonist along with acetazolamide to start lowering the intraocular pressure while I arrange emergent ophthalmology consultation, since she will likely need definitive treatment such as laser iridotomy. I would not treat this as simple conjunctivitis and send her home with antibiotic drops, because that would delay definitive care and put her vision at real risk.

title: EMS Handover for a Suspected STEMI with Deteriorating Vitals
reading_stem: Paramedics call ahead with a patient experiencing crushing chest pain for 45 minutes with a prehospital ECG showing ST elevation in the anterior leads. On arrival, the paramedic gives a verbal handover while the patient is being transferred to the monitor. The patient appears pale and diaphoretic.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate actively listens to the full prehospital handover including vitals trend, treatments given such as aspirin and nitroglycerin, and response to those treatments, allow the handover to convey that blood pressure has been trending down over the last several minutes. If the candidate repeats the ECG immediately on arrival rather than relying solely on the prehospital tracing, confirm ongoing anterior ST elevation and now new hypotension. If the candidate recognizes cardiogenic shock physiology developing and avoids further nitroglycerin given the hypotension, this is correct since nitrates can worsen hypotension in a hypotensive STEMI. If the candidate activates the cardiac catheterization lab immediately based on the prehospital ECG without waiting for a repeat ECG in the department, that is also an acceptable and often preferred practice to save time to reperfusion, and should be recognized as appropriate. If the candidate delays activation to repeat unnecessary tests, interject that time to reperfusion is being lost and ask the candidate to reconsider. Expect discussion of starting inotropic or vasopressor support cautiously if hypotension worsens, clear closed loop communication with the cath lab team, and continued reassessment during the handover process rather than treating handover as a passive event.
checklist: Actively engages with the EMS handover, capturing vitals trends and treatments already given rather than treating it passively
Confirms the STEMI with a repeat ECG in the department or activates the cath lab promptly based on the prehospital ECG
Recognizes evolving cardiogenic shock and avoids nitroglycerin in the setting of hypotension
Activates the cardiac catheterization lab without unnecessary delay, prioritizing time to reperfusion
Communicates clearly and in closed loop fashion with the receiving team and considers cautious hemodynamic support if needed
model_answer: I am listening carefully to the full prehospital handover, not just the ECG finding, because the trend that his blood pressure has been dropping over the last several minutes changes my management significantly and suggests early cardiogenic shock. Given the clear anterior ST elevation on the prehospital ECG and his ongoing symptoms, I would activate the cardiac catheterization lab immediately rather than waiting to repeat an ECG in the department, since time to reperfusion is critical and repeating it should not delay activation. Because he is now hypotensive, I am specifically avoiding further nitroglycerin, which could worsen his blood pressure and push him further into shock. I would prepare for cautious fluid or vasopressor support if his pressure continues to drop while arranging transfer to the cath lab. Throughout this I am communicating clearly in closed loop fashion with both the paramedics and the cath lab team so nothing gets lost in the handover.

title: Simultaneous Arrival of Two Critical Patients After a Collision
reading_stem: Two patients arrive simultaneously from a two vehicle collision. Patient A is a 40 year old man who is talking but has an obviously deformed open femur fracture with brisk bleeding. Patient B is a 25 year old woman who is unresponsive with shallow breathing and a rapid, thready pulse. Only one resuscitation bay and team are immediately available.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate quickly performs a rapid triage assessment of both patients rather than fully assessing one before glancing at the other, confirm that patient A, despite dramatic bleeding, is talking and protecting his airway, while patient B has an unprotected airway and signs of shock, making her the higher immediate priority for the resuscitation bay. If the candidate directs a team member to apply a tourniquet and direct pressure to patient A's leg while personally moving to manage patient B's airway and circulation, allow this parallel task delegation to proceed effectively. If the candidate becomes fixated on patient A's dramatic bleeding and neglects patient B, have patient B's oxygen saturation and mental status decline further to illustrate the cost of misallocated attention in a multiple patient scenario. If the candidate calls for additional resources such as more staff, a second bay, or trauma team activation for both patients, this reflects appropriate recognition of the scale of the situation. Expect ongoing reassessment and reprioritization as both patients' conditions evolve, along with clear task delegation and communication using structured language so the team understands who is responsible for what.
checklist: Performs rapid simultaneous triage rather than fully managing one patient before assessing the other
Correctly identifies which patient is the higher immediate priority based on airway and shock status rather than visual drama of injury
Delegates tasks effectively to manage both patients in parallel using available staff
Calls for additional resources appropriate to the scale of the situation
Continuously reassesses and reprioritizes as both patients' conditions evolve
model_answer: With two critical patients arriving at once I need to rapidly triage both before committing fully to either one, and even though patient A's open femur fracture looks dramatic, he is talking and protecting his airway, while patient B is unresponsive with a compromised airway and signs of shock, which makes her my higher immediate priority. I would delegate a team member to apply a tourniquet and direct pressure to patient A's leg while I personally move to manage patient B's airway and circulation, so both patients are being addressed in parallel rather than sequentially. I am calling for additional staff and resources right away given the scale of this situation, because trying to manage both patients with a single team will not work. I am giving clear, specific instructions rather than vague requests, so everyone knows exactly what they are responsible for. Throughout this I am reassessing both patients frequently, because priorities can shift quickly and I do not want to become fixated on the more visually dramatic injury at the expense of the sicker patient.

title: Missed Torsion Diagnosis Requiring Disclosure and Quality Review
reading_stem: A 15 year old boy was seen yesterday by a colleague for scrotal pain and discharged with a diagnosis of epididymitis. He returns today with worsening pain, and on your exam you find a high riding, horizontal testis with absent cremasteric reflex, concerning for testicular torsion missed on the prior visit.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate immediately arranges urgent urology consultation and, if available, bedside or formal ultrasound with Doppler to confirm torsion without delaying surgical consultation for imaging, allow urology to be paged and the patient taken emergently to the operating room, though with a testis that may not be salvageable given the delay. If the candidate recognizes the need for open, honest disclosure to the patient and family about the missed diagnosis on the prior visit, expect the candidate to verbalize a disclosure conversation that is honest, empathetic, avoids blaming the previous physician personally, and does not minimize what happened. If the candidate avoids disclosure or suggests withholding information about the prior visit, interject that this is not appropriate practice and ask the candidate to reconsider. If the candidate discusses reporting this case through a formal quality improvement or morbidity and mortality process rather than simply mentioning it informally to the colleague, this reflects correct systems based thinking. Expect discussion of how to approach the colleague using a nonpunitive, systems focused framework aimed at understanding what led to the missed diagnosis rather than assigning individual blame, and how this could inform a broader process change such as a standardized red flag checklist for scrotal pain presentations.
checklist: Prioritizes urgent surgical or urology involvement for actual patient care first, without delaying for administrative concerns
Recognizes the need for honest, empathetic disclosure of the missed diagnosis to the patient and family
Avoids blaming the previous physician personally during disclosure or in initial discussion
Reports the case through a formal quality improvement or morbidity and mortality process rather than handling it informally
Approaches the case using nonpunitive, systems based thinking aimed at preventing recurrence
model_answer: My first priority is still this patient's care, so I am getting urology involved emergently and pursuing imaging only if it will not meaningfully delay operative management, since testicular torsion is time critical regardless of what happened yesterday. Separately, I know this family deserves honest disclosure that torsion was not diagnosed on the prior visit, and I would have that conversation directly and empathetically, acknowledging what happened without minimizing it and without personally blaming my colleague in front of the family. After the immediate care is handled, I would make sure this case gets reviewed through our formal quality improvement or morbidity and mortality process rather than just mentioning it informally to my colleague, because a single conversation does not create systems level learning. My goal in that review is understanding what factors contributed to the missed diagnosis, such as whether a standardized approach to scrotal pain was followed, rather than assigning blame to one individual. Ultimately I want this case to drive a concrete process change, like a checklist or a clearer pathway for scrotal pain presentations, so the same error is less likely to happen again.

title: Applying a Clinical Decision Rule to a Low Risk Chest Pain Patient
reading_stem: A 45 year old man with atypical chest pain and a normal ECG asks whether he needs further cardiac testing before going home. He read online about a blood test that can rule out a blood clot in the lungs and asks if that applies to him, since his main complaint today is pleuritic chest pain, not classic cardiac pain.
examiner_scenario: If the candidate clarifies the actual presenting complaint and pretest probability for pulmonary embolism using a validated tool such as the PERC rule or Wells criteria, allow the scenario to establish that he is genuinely low risk with no major risk factors. If the candidate correctly explains that a decision rule like PERC is only valid when applied to patients who are already low pretest probability, and that a negative PERC in a truly low risk patient allows PE to be excluded without further testing, this reflects correct application of the rule and its intended population. If the candidate proposes applying PERC indiscriminately to a higher risk patient or misunderstands that it only rules out disease in an appropriately selected low risk population, interject with a data point revealing he actually has several risk factors that push him out of the low risk category, testing whether the candidate recognizes the rule no longer applies and further testing such as D-dimer or CT is needed. If the candidate discusses the underlying evidence, such as the derivation and validation studies behind the rule and its sensitivity in the appropriate population, this demonstrates genuine critical appraisal rather than rote rule application. Expect the candidate to communicate this clearly and honestly to the patient, explaining both what the test can and cannot tell them and what shared decision making looks like for further workup or reassurance.
checklist: Clarifies the presenting complaint and establishes pretest probability before applying any clinical decision rule
Correctly explains that a rule such as PERC is only valid in an appropriately selected low pretest probability population
Recognizes when a patient does not meet criteria for a rule to be applied and adjusts the workup accordingly
Demonstrates understanding of the evidence behind the decision rule rather than applying it by rote
Communicates the reasoning and limitations of testing clearly to the patient in a shared decision making conversation
model_answer: Before I answer his question about the blood clot test, I need to actually establish his pretest probability for pulmonary embolism, because a rule like PERC is only valid when it is applied to patients who are already low risk to begin with, it is not a universal rule out test for anyone with chest pain. If his history and exam genuinely put him in a low risk category with no major risk factors, then a negative PERC would actually be enough to exclude PE without needing a D-dimer or CT scan, and I would explain that reasoning to him clearly. If instead he has risk factors I was not initially aware of that push him out of the low risk category, then PERC no longer applies to him and I would need to move on to a D-dimer or imaging depending on his risk level. I want to understand the actual evidence behind this rule, including the population it was validated in, rather than just applying it mechanically to every chest pain patient. Finally I would explain all of this to him honestly, including what the test can and cannot tell us, so we can make a shared decision about further workup together.
